nodes.label: Ardashir I
nodes.full: Ardashir, ruler of Fars, defeated the last Arsacid at Hormizdagan in 224, was crowned in 226 and by 230 had taken the old Parthian lands to the Euphrates, with new capitals at Ardashir-Khwarra (Firuzabad) and Ctesiphon, and the title Shahanshah, King of Kings of the Iranians; he built a centralised state with the Zoroastrian priesthood as its ally, and attacked Roman Mesopotamia in 230–232.
nodes.src: Tabari, History; Touraj Daryaee, Sasanian Persia (2009); Josef Wiesehöfer, Ancient Persia (1996).

nodes.label: Shapur I
nodes.full: Shapur I, who succeeded his father Ardashir, invaded Syria in 252–253 and 256, sacked Antioch and Dura-Europos, defeated and captured the emperor Valerian in 260, left a trilingual inscription of his deeds (Res Gestae Divi Saporis) on the Ka'ba-ye Zardosht at Naqsh-e Rostam, founded Bishapur and Gundeshapur with Roman prisoners and gave Mani leave to teach.
nodes.src: Res Gestae Divi Saporis (ŠKZ); Michael Back; Daryaee 2009; Ammianus 23.5; Lactantius, De mortibus persecutorum 5.

nodes.label: Diocletian and Galerius
nodes.full: Diocletian, an Illyrian soldier who took the throne in 284 and divided power in the Tetrarchy, made the East his own, strengthened the Strata Diocletiana and the limes of Syria, Mesopotamia and Arabia; Galerius, his Caesar, was defeated by Narseh in 296 near Carrhae but crushed him in 298, captured his harem and treasure, and in the Peace of Nisibis of 299 took five trans-Tigrine provinces and the protectorate of Armenia and Iberia.
nodes.src: Peter the Patrician, fr. 13–14; Ammianus; Fergus Millar, The Roman Near East 31 BC–AD 337 (1993); Timothy Barnes, Constantine and Eusebius (1981).

nodes.label: Shapur II
nodes.full: Shapur II, king from before his birth, who was crowned as an infant in 309 and ruled for seventy years, put down the Arab raiders, took Armenia, besieged Nisibis three times, fought a long war with Constantius II in 337–361 and, in the war of Julian's invasion of 363, forced Jovian to cede Nisibis and the five provinces, and presided over the compiling of the Avesta and the persecutions of the Christians.
nodes.src: Ammianus Marcellinus 16–25; Tabari; Daryaee 2009; Richard Frye, in The Cambridge History of Iran vol. 3 (1983).

nodes.label: Constantine and Constantius II
nodes.full: Constantine, after the defeat of his rivals in 324, set himself up as protector of the Christians of Persia and prepared an eastern campaign for 337, when he died at Nicomedia; his son Constantius II fought the Persians in a series of inconclusive wars and sieges of Nisibis (338, 346, 350) while the Sasanians attacked Roman Mesopotamia, Singara and Amida in 359.
nodes.src: Eusebius, Vita Constantini 4.8–13; Ammianus 18–19; Barnes 1981; Michael Whitby in The Cambridge Ancient History vol. 13 (1998).

nodes.label: Kavad I and Khusrau I
nodes.full: Kavad I, restored by the Hephthalites after being deposed in 496, fought Anastasius in 502–506 and Justin in 524–531 and patronised the communist-leaning Mazdak movement before turning on it; his son Khusrau I (531–579) reformed the taxation and army with a cadastral survey, the dihgans' service, the Eternal Peace of 532, the sack of Antioch in 540, the conquests in Yemen and Lazica and the cultural revival with Greek and Indian learning.
nodes.src: Procopius, Wars 1–2; Agathias; Tabari; Daryaee 2009; Parvaneh Pourshariati, Decline and Fall of the Sasanian Empire (2008).

nodes.label: Justinian
nodes.full: Justinian, who restored the western provinces by his generals Belisarius and Narses and codified the law, fought Persia in 527–532 and 540–562 with the dual aims of securing the eastern frontier and of using peace payments to free his armies; the Eternal Peace of 532 and the Fifty Years' Peace of 562, in which he agreed to pay 30,000 gold coins a year, left him free in Italy.
nodes.src: Procopius, Wars 1–2, Secret History; Menander the Guardsman; Geoffrey Greatrex and Samuel Lieu, The Roman Eastern Frontier and the Persian Wars vol. 2 (2002).

nodes.label: Khusrau II
nodes.full: Khusrau II, restored to the throne in 591 by the emperor Maurice after the usurpation of Bahram Chobin, swore revenge when Maurice was murdered by Phocas in 602, and conquered Mesopotamia, Syria, Palestine and Egypt, reached Chalcedon in 617 and 626, built the great palace of Dastagird and amassed gold and treasures; after Heraclius' invasion he was deposed and killed by his son Kavad II in February 628.
nodes.src: Theophylact Simocatta; Sebeos; Chronicon Paschale; Theophanes; James Howard-Johnston, Witnesses to a World Crisis (2010).

nodes.label: Maurice, Phocas and Heraclius
nodes.full: Maurice (582–602), who put Khusrau II on the throne and gained Armenia, was murdered with his sons by Phocas, whose tyranny set off the Persian invasion; Heraclius, son of the exarch of Africa, overthrew Phocas in 610, was almost beaten in 618–622, then led the campaigns of 622–628 that brought Khusrau's fall, and restored the Cross in Jerusalem in 630.
nodes.src: Theophylact; Chronicon Paschale; Walter Kaegi, Heraclius, Emperor of Byzantium (2003); Howard-Johnston 2010.

nodes.label: Lakhmids and Ghassanids
nodes.full: The Lakhmid kings of al-Hira, such as al-Mundhir III (505–554), who was killed in battle by the Ghassanids in 554, were clients of Persia, patrons of poetry and Christians of the Church of the East; the Ghassanid phylarchs, led by al-Harith ibn Jabala (529–569) and al-Mundhir (569–582), were the empire's Miaphysite Arab allies, whose fall in 582 and the Lakhmids' end in 602 removed the buffer states before the Arab conquests.
nodes.src: Procopius, Wars 1–2; John of Ephesus; Irfan Shahid, Byzantium and the Arabs vols. 1–3 (1984–1995); Ibn al-Kalbi.

nodes.label: Armenia, Iberia and Albania
nodes.full: Armenia, Iberia and Albania, which had been Arsacid and Roman-aligned, were divided between Sasanian and Roman influence by the partition of 387, with the larger share to Persia; the Sasanians' attempts to force Zoroastrianism led to the rising of Vardan Mamikonian at Avarayr in 451, which led to the religious freedom granted in the Treaty of Nvarsak in 484, while the Roman emperors used Armenia and Lazica for recruiting soldiers.
nodes.src: Elishe, History of Vardan and the Armenian War; Lazar of P'arpi; Nina Garsoïan in The Armenian People vol. 1 (1997); Cyril Toumanoff, Studies in Christian Caucasian History (1963).

nodes.label: Capture of Valerian
nodes.full: In 260 Shapur I defeated the Roman army near Edessa and captured the emperor Valerian, with the Praetorian Prefect and many senators; the emperor's humiliation, shown on the rock reliefs of Naqsh-e Rostam, Bishapur and Darabgird, in which Philip the Arab kneels and Valerian is taken by the wrist, is the single largest disaster of a Roman emperor, and he died in captivity, as Lactantius says, flayed and stuffed.
nodes.src: Res Gestae Divi Saporis 18–22; Lactantius, De mortibus 5; Zosimus 1.36; Naqsh-e Rostam and Bishapur reliefs; Michael Whitby, Rome at War (2002).

nodes.label: Odaenathus and Zenobia
nodes.full: After Valerian's capture Odaenathus, the lord of Palmyra, drove the Persians back from Roman territory in 262–267 and was granted a Roman command of the East; his widow Zenobia took Egypt and Anatolia in 270–271 and declared her son Vaballathus Augustus, until Aurelian defeated her at Antioch and Emesa in 272 and razed Palmyra after a revolt in 273.
nodes.src: Zosimus 1.39–61; Historia Augusta, Tyranni Triginta; Palmyrene inscriptions; Pat Southern, Empress Zenobia (2008).

nodes.label: Narseh’s war
nodes.full: Narseh, who had seized the throne from Bahram III and lost Armenia, attacked in 296 and defeated Galerius between Carrhae and Callinicum, but in 298 Galerius surprised his camp in Armenia, wounding the king and taking his wives, sisters and children; the Peace of Nisibis, negotiated in 299 by the diplomats Sicorius Probus and Apharban, gave Rome five trans-Tigritane satrapies and the right to name the king of Iberia.
nodes.src: Peter the Patrician fr. 14; Paikuli inscription; Eutropius 9.24–25; Ammianus 25.7.9; Barnes 1981.

nodes.label: Julian’s expedition
nodes.full: Julian led an army of 65,000 down the Euphrates in March 363 and reached Ctesiphon, burned his ships and moved up the Tigris instead of attacking the capital; he was killed in a skirmish near Samarra on 26 June, probably by a Persian spear, and his successor Jovian, with a starving army, ceded Nisibis, Singara and the five provinces to Shapur II in a peace of thirty years.
nodes.src: Ammianus 23–25; Libanius, Orations 17–18; Zosimus 3; Gregory Nazianzen, Orations 4–5; Glen Bowersock, Julian the Apostate (1978).

nodes.label: Amida and Dara
nodes.full: Kavad I, claiming unpaid subsidies for the defence of the Caspian Gates, took Theodosiopolis in 502 and Amida in January 503 after a siege of three months; Anastasius sent armies, and after three years of fighting the two sides made a seven-year truce in 506, with the Romans building the fortress of Dara in 505–507 on the border, a cause of the dispute for years.
nodes.src: Joshua the Stylite, Chronicle; Procopius, Wars 1.7–10; Greatrex and Lieu 2002.

nodes.label: Sack of Antioch
nodes.full: Khusrau I broke the Eternal Peace in 540, took Sura, Beroea and Hierapolis and in June besieged Antioch, taking the third city of the empire after a short assault, plundering its churches, taking thousands of its people to found a new city, Veh Antiok Khusrau (Rumagan), near Ctesiphon, and collecting large sums of gold from the cities of Syria and Mesopotamia.
nodes.src: Procopius, Wars 2.5–14; Malalas 17; Evagrius, Ecclesiastical History 4.25–26; Greatrex and Lieu 2002.

nodes.label: Lazic war
nodes.full: The kingdom of Lazica on the east coast of the Black Sea, a Roman client, passed in 541 to Persian protection, and in a war of two decades the Romans and Persians fought for Petra, Archaeopolis and the passes, on the road to the Caspian; the war ended in the Fifty Years' Peace of 562, which left Lazica to the Romans for a payment of 30,000 solidi a year.
nodes.src: Procopius, Wars 2.15–30, 8; Agathias 2–4; Menander fr. 6; Greatrex and Lieu 2002.

nodes.label: Persian conquests
nodes.full: Under Khusrau II's generals Shahrbaraz, Shahin and Farrukhan, Persian armies took Antioch in 611, Damascus in 613, Jerusalem in May 614 with a massacre of the Christians, as the Chronicle of Sebeos and Strategios record, and carried off the True Cross, and Alexandria in 619, Egypt's last Roman city, and Chalcedon opposite Constantinople in 617; the Persian empire reached the extent of the Achaemenids.
nodes.src: Sebeos; Strategios of Mar Saba; Chronicon Paschale; John of Nikiu; Howard-Johnston 2010; Kaegi 2003.

nodes.label: Siege of Constantinople
nodes.full: In the summer of 626 a Persian army under Shahrbaraz at Chalcedon and an Avar-Slav-Bulgar force of the khagan before the Theodosian walls besieged Constantinople; under the patriarch Sergius and Bonus the city, with the icon of the Virgin carried on the walls, resisted for ten days, and on 7–8 August the Avar fleet of dugouts was destroyed in the Golden Horn and the allies left; the failure marked a turning-point of the war.
nodes.src: Chronicon Paschale 716–726; Theodore Synkellos; George of Pisidia, Bellum Avaricum; James Howard-Johnston, Witnesses to a World Crisis (2010).

nodes.label: Heraclius at Nineveh
nodes.full: Heraclius, having made peace with the Avars, led an army through the Black Sea to Armenia and the Caucasus in 622–624 and then in 627, with Turkic Khazar allies, moved into Mesopotamia, defeated the Persian general Rhahzadh at Nineveh on 12 December 627 and marched on Dastagird, plundering the palace; Khusrau fled and was killed in February 628, and his son Kavad II made peace, restoring all the territories.
nodes.src: Theophanes AM 6113–6120; George of Pisidia, Heraclias; Kaegi 2003; Howard-Johnston 2010.

nodes.label: Sasanian state and reform
nodes.full: The Sasanian state, as it appears in Persian traditions recorded in Arabic and Middle Persian texts, was a hierarchy of a king of kings, the great houses and a landed gentry (dihqans) with an army of cavalry, with four estates of priests, warriors, scribes and commoners; Khusrau I's reform divided the empire into four military quarters under spahbeds, fixed a land and poll tax, and set up a bureaucracy of the royal secretaries.
nodes.src: Tabari; Letter of Tansar; Ibn al-Muqaffa'; Pourshariati 2008; Daryaee 2009.

nodes.label: Roman diocese and frontier army
nodes.full: Diocletian divided the East into dioceses of Oriens and Egypt under the praetorian prefect and a duke on each frontier sector, with a field army (comitatenses) under the master of soldiers and the limitanei in the forts; in the sixth century Justinian made the dukes of Mesopotamia, Armenia and Phoenicia responsible for fortifications, and set up a magister militum per Armeniam.
nodes.src: Notitia Dignitatum; Codex Justinianus; A. H. M. Jones, The Later Roman Empire (1964); Whitby 2002.

nodes.label: Eternal Peace and Fifty Years’ Peace
nodes.full: In 532 the emperor Justinian, to free his hands for the West, made an Eternal Peace with Khusrau I and paid 11,000 pounds of gold; after the war of 540–561 a fifty years' treaty in 562, negotiated by Peter the Patrician and Zich, allowed the Persians a payment of 30,000 solidi a year, stopped Persian interference in the Roman Armenia and Lazica, and set out a long list of trade, religion and diplomatic rights in the text recorded by Menander.
nodes.src: Procopius, Wars 1.22; Menander the Guardsman fr. 6; Greatrex and Lieu 2002.

nodes.label: Peace of Jovian
nodes.full: Jovian, to bring his starving army back, concluded in July 363 a thirty years' truce, ceding the five trans-Tigrine provinces taken in 298, including the great fortress city of Nisibis, which was evacuated by its citizens, with Singara and Castra Maurorum, and abandoning Armenia to Persian influence; some contemporaries and later writers likened the humiliation to the Caudine Forks.
nodes.src: Ammianus 25.7–9; Zosimus 3.31; Libanius, Oration 18; Whitby 2002.

nodes.label: Kartir
nodes.full: The priest Kartir, adviser to Shapur I, Hormizd I, Bahram I and II, and grand mobed, set up fire temples throughout the empire and, in his inscriptions on the Ka'ba-ye Zardosht and at Naqsh-e Rajab, boasts of having persecuted Jews, Buddhists, Hindus, Nazarenes, Christians, baptisers and Manichaeans; the death of Mani about 276 was his work.
nodes.src: Kartir's inscriptions (KKZ, KNRm, KSM); Mary Boyce, A History of Zoroastrianism vol. 3 (1991); David Neil MacKenzie, ‘Kerdir's Inscription’ (1989).

nodes.label: Mani
nodes.full: Mani, born in Babylonia in 216 to a Parthian family and raised in a baptising sect, proclaimed himself the Seal of the Prophets in 240, was patronised by Shapur I, wrote the Shabuhragan for him and sent missionaries to the Roman empire, India and Central Asia; he was imprisoned and died in Gundeshapur about 276 under Bahram I, but his religion spread across Eurasia and lasted to the sixteenth century.
nodes.src: Cologne Mani Codex; Kephalaia; Iain Gardner and Samuel Lieu, Manichaean Texts from the Roman Empire (2004); Samuel Lieu, Manichaeism in Mesopotamia and the Roman East (1994).

nodes.label: Persian martyrs
nodes.full: The Christians of Persia, deportees from Roman Syria and Mesopotamia and native converts, were suspected as a fifth column of Rome, and under Shapur II in the Forty Years' Persecution, from 339, the catholicos Simeon bar Sabbae was executed and tens of thousands were killed; the Synod of Isaac in 410 organised the Church of the East under a catholicos of Seleucia-Ctesiphon, which became Nestorian in 486 and 497.
nodes.src: Acts of the Persian Martyrs; Synodicon Orientale (ed. Chabot, 1902); Sebastian Brock, ‘Christians in the Sasanian Empire’ (1982); Aphrahat, Demonstrations.

nodes.label: Babylonian Talmud
nodes.full: The Jewish academies of Sura, Pumbedita and Nehardea, under the exilarch, developed the Babylonian Talmud, a great commentary on the Mishnah, in generations of rabbis from Rav and Samuel in the early third century to Ravina and Rav Ashi in the fifth, and its final redaction by the saboraim in the sixth; the Persian kings were mostly tolerant, with an occasional persecution, as under Yazdgerd II and Peroz.
nodes.src: Babylonian Talmud; Jacob Neusner, A History of the Jews in Babylonia vols. 2–5 (1966–1970); Isaiah Gafni.

nodes.label: Mazdak
nodes.full: Mazdak, a priest who taught that the wealth, women and property of the rich should be held in common to end the strife, had the support of Kavad I in the 490s, which turned the nobility and clergy against the king, who was deposed in 496; Khusrau I, with Zoroastrian orthodoxy, suppressed the sect in 528 and killed its leaders.
nodes.src: Tabari; Nizam al-Mulk, Siyasatnama; Patricia Crone, ‘Kavad's Heresy and Mazdak's Revolt’, Iran 29 (1991).

nodes.label: Rock reliefs of Shapur
nodes.full: Shapur I and his successors carved on the cliffs of Naqsh-e Rostam, Bishapur and Darabgird the triumph over Rome: Valerian is led by the wrist, Gordian III lies beneath the horse and Philip the Arab kneels, in reliefs that show the king as the equal of the Achaemenids, whose tombs are on the same cliff, and which recall the defeat in a monumental form that Rome's reliefs did not.
nodes.src: Bishapur reliefs; Naqsh-e Rostam; Georgina Herrmann, The Iranian Revival (1977); Matthew Canepa, The Two Eyes of the Earth (2009).

nodes.label: Taq-e Kasra
nodes.full: The great iwan of Ctesiphon, usually called Taq-e Kasra, with a vault of 25 metres span and 37 metres high, the widest unreinforced brick vault in the world, built probably under Khusrau I with the prisoners of Antioch or under Khusrau II, was the throne hall of the palace and the model of Persian court architecture; its carpet, the Spring of Khusrau, was taken as plunder by the Arabs in 637.
nodes.src: Tabari; Ernst Kühnel, Ctesiphon (1933); Daryaee 2009; Michael Morony, Iraq after the Muslim Conquest (1984).

nodes.label: Sasanian silver
nodes.full: Gilded silver bowls, plates and ewers with scenes of the king hunting lions, banqueting with musicians and dancers and fighting, struck with the royal stamps and weights of the treasury, were among the best known of the court's products; the Sasanian hunting plates were exported to Central Asia, China and the Byzantine empire, where they were copied.
nodes.src: Prudence Harper, Silver Vessels of the Sasanian Period vol. 1 (1981); Daryaee 2009; British Museum and Hermitage holdings.

nodes.label: Ephrem and Narsai
nodes.full: Ephrem the Syrian (c. 306–373), deacon of Nisibis and then of Edessa after its cession in 363, wrote hymns, commentaries and homilies in Syriac that made him the greatest poet of Syriac Christianity; Narsai (d. 502), the head of the school of Nisibis, and Jacob of Serugh composed verse homilies, and the Syriac of Mesopotamia became a literary language of the church across the Roman and Persian frontier.
nodes.src: Ephrem, Hymns on Paradise, Carmina Nisibena; Sebastian Brock, The Luminous Eye (1985); Brock, The Hidden Pearl (2001).

nodes.label: Gundeshapur
nodes.full: Gundeshapur, a city founded by Shapur I in Khuzestan with Roman prisoners, held under Khusrau I a medical school and hospital where Greek, Indian and Persian learning was taught, which was joined by the Greek philosophers who left Athens when Justinian closed the Academy in 529, and in the later tradition it was the source of the transmission of Greek medicine to Islam.
nodes.src: Tabari; Ibn Abi Usaybi'a, Uyun al-anba; Agathias 2.30–31; Daryaee 2009; Michael Dols, ‘The Origins of the Islamic Hospital’, Bulletin of the History of Medicine 61 (1987).

nodes.label: School of Nisibis
nodes.full: When the Roman city of Nisibis was ceded to Persia in 363, its Syriac Christian school moved to Edessa under Ephrem and was refounded about 489 by Narsai in Nisibis, with statutes about 496 that regulated life as a monastic university with a head, teachers and several hundred students, which taught the Bible commentaries of Theodore of Mopsuestia and was the main school of the Church of the East.
nodes.src: Statutes of the School of Nisibis (trans. Vööbus, 1962); Adam Becker, Fear of God and the Beginning of Wisdom (2006).

nodes.label: Procopius
nodes.full: Procopius of Caesarea, legal adviser to Belisarius, wrote the Wars in eight books on the campaigns against the Persians, Vandals and Goths, the Buildings on Justinian's works and the Secret History, a hostile account of the court; his account of the Persian war of 527–553 and of Khusrau, and the account of the plague in 542, is the main source for the period.
nodes.src: Procopius, Wars, Buildings, Secret History; Averil Cameron, Procopius and the Sixth Century (1985); Anthony Kaldellis, Procopius of Caesarea (2004).

nodes.label: Khwaday-namag
nodes.full: The Book of Kings (Khwaday-namag), a Middle Persian chronicle compiled under Khusrau I and Khusrau II from the oral lore of the Persian kings back to the legendary Kayanids and down to Yazdgerd III, which has not survived, was translated into Arabic by Ibn al-Muqaffa' in the eighth century and became the basis for Firdausi's Shahnameh and Tabari's account of the Persian kings.
nodes.src: Ibn al-Muqaffa'; Tabari; Firdausi, Shahnameh; Daryaee 2009; Zeev Rubin.

nodes.label: Silk and Justinian’s silkworms
nodes.full: The Roman state, concerned at the price of silk, which came through Persia and Central Asia, limited the places of trade to Nisibis, Callinicum and Artaxata by the treaties from 408, and Justinian, who failed in 531 to open a route by Ethiopian traders, in 552 had two monks from Central Asia carry silkworm eggs hidden in hollow canes to Constantinople, which began an independent European silk industry.
nodes.src: Procopius, Wars 8.17; Menander fr. 10; Theophanes of Byzantium; Codex Justinianus 4.63.4.

nodes.label: Tribute and frontier trade
nodes.full: The treaties of 299 and 562 set out the places at which merchants could pass the frontier and the customs duties (the commercium), which the two states used to control the trade in silk, spices and precious stones; for the defence of the Caspian Gates Rome paid Persia for years, and the tribute and subsidies, which by 562 reached 30,000 solidi a year, were the main fiscal link between the empires.
nodes.src: Peter the Patrician fr. 14; Menander fr. 6; Codex Justinianus 4.63.4; Greatrex and Lieu 2002.

nodes.label: Red Sea and India trade
nodes.full: The Persian Gulf and Red Sea trade, with Aksum on the Ethiopian coast as the Roman partner and the Persians' control of the ports of the Gulf and Ceylon (as Cosmas Indicopleustes notes in about 550), brought spices, pepper and ivory from India and Africa; the Sasanian conquest of Yemen about 570 was an attempt to control the southern end of the route.
nodes.src: Cosmas Indicopleustes, Christian Topography; Procopius, Wars 1.19–20; Tabari; Daryaee 2009.

nodes.label: Dara
nodes.full: Anastasius built, in the three years after the war of 502–506, a fortress city at Dara on the Mesopotamian frontier, 5 kilometres from Nisibis, with a double wall, a great defence tower, a dam and cisterns, and reconstructed it under Justinian; the Persians objected that it broke the treaties against building fortifications on the frontier, and its defeat of Persian assault in 530 under the general Belisarius (the battle of Dara) is the most famous action.
nodes.src: Procopius, Wars 1.13–14, Buildings 2.1–3; Zacharias of Mytilene; Greatrex and Lieu 2002.

nodes.label: Band-e Kaisar
nodes.full: The Band-e Kaisar, the Caesar's Dam, at Shushtar on the Karun, a weir of 500 metres with arches, a canal tunnel and a system of water mills that irrigated the plain of Khuzestan, is said by tradition to have been built by the Roman prisoners of Valerian's defeated army under Shapur I, and is a masterpiece of Roman hydraulic engineering in Persian service.
nodes.src: Tabari; Ibn Hawqal; Daryaee 2009; Norman Smith, A History of Dams (1971); UNESCO World Heritage listing (2009).

nodes.label: Burzoe, chess and Kalila
nodes.full: Under Khusrau I the physician Burzoe, who is said to have gone to India for the Panchatantra and brought back the game of chess (chatrang) and the book of Kalila and Dimna, translated into Middle Persian, was part of the cultural revival; Sasanian games of backgammon (nard) and chess entered the later Arabic world.
nodes.src: Kalila wa Dimna; Burzoe's introduction (Shahnameh); Daryaee 2009; Harold Murray, A History of Chess (1913).

nodes.label: The two eyes
nodes.full: The Roman and Persian courts, in a tradition of mutual recognition and ritual, treated each other as the two lamps or eyes of the world and exchanged embassies at accessions with letters of brotherhood, such as Khusrau's to Maurice and Justin II's to Chosroes; the idea of the two empires as the two eyes of the world is in Persian and Greek sources of the fifth to seventh centuries.
nodes.src: Menander fr. 6; Theophylact 4.11; Peter the Patrician fr. 13; Canepa 2009.

nodes.label: Hephthalites and Turks
nodes.full: The Hephthalites (White Huns), who held Bactria from about 440 and defeated and killed Peroz in 484, forced Persia to pay them tribute for decades, until Khusrau I, with the help of the Turkic Western Turks, destroyed them about 560, so bringing the Turks to the frontiers of Iran and sending their first embassies to Constantinople in 568.
nodes.src: Procopius, Wars 1.3–4; Menander fr. 10; Étienne de la Vaissière, Sogdian Traders (2005); Daryaee 2009.

nodes.label: Aksum, Himyar and Yemen
nodes.full: The Jewish king of Himyar Dhu Nuwas persecuted the Christians of Najran in 523, and Kaleb of Aksum, at Justin I's request, invaded Yemen in 525; Abraha, the Aksumite governor, claimed the lordship in 540s, and Persian forces under Wahriz expelled the Ethiopians about 570, making Yemen a Sasanian province, and a prelude to the Prophet's Arabia.
nodes.src: Procopius, Wars 1.19–20; Martyrdom of Arethas; Ibn Ishaq, Sira; Irfan Shahid, The Martyrs of Najran (1971).

nodes.label: Plague of Justinian
nodes.full: Plague appeared at Pelusium in 541 and reached Constantinople in the spring of 542, where, according to Procopius, 10,000 a day died in the peak, and it spread through the Roman and Persian empires to the West, with deaths in the millions in the first outbreaks and returns for two centuries; Persia suffered too, and Khusrau I's army was weakened.
nodes.src: Procopius, Wars 2.22–23; John of Ephesus; Evagrius 4.29; Lester Little (ed.), Plague and the End of Antiquity (2007); Peter Sarris.

nodes.label: Dust veil and Antioch earthquake
nodes.full: The earthquake of 29 May 526 destroyed Antioch, killing, according to Malalas, 250,000 people, and the sun's dimming in 536, after a volcanic eruption, in the accounts of Procopius, John of Ephesus and Cassiodorus, brought a time of cold summers, crop failures and famine in the Mediterranean and Near East, which followed by plague in the 540s.
nodes.src: Malalas 17.16; Procopius, Wars 4.14.5; Michael Baillie, Exodus to Arthur (1999); Ulf Büntgen et al., Nature Geoscience (2016).

nodes.label: Deportations and new cities
nodes.full: The Sasanian kings founded new cities and transported populations from the Roman provinces, among them the captives of Antioch in 256 and 540, who were settled at Gundeshapur and Veh Antiok Khusrau, of Apamea in 540 and of Dara in 573, with Christian and Greek-speaking communities that supplied the craftsmen of the royal works and a cause of the spread of Christianity in Persia.
nodes.src: Procopius, Wars 2.9, 2.14; Shapur I, Res Gestae; Daryaee 2009; Morony 1984.

nodes.label: Purandokht and Azarmidokht
nodes.full: After the murder of Kavad II's son Ardashir III by the general Shahrbaraz in 630, the daughters of Khusrau II, Purandokht (Boran) and Azarmidokht, were crowned as queens, struck coins in their own names and put the empire into some order for two years; Khusrau's queen Shirin, an Aramean Christian who built a monastery and is celebrated in the Persian poets, had been a power at the court.
nodes.src: Tabari; Sebeos; coins of Boran and Azarmidokht; Daryaee 2009; Nizami, Khusrau and Shirin.

nodes.label: Prisoners of Valerian
nodes.full: The tens of thousands of Roman soldiers and civilians taken by Shapur I were settled in Fars, Parthia and Khuzestan in cities he founded, and worked on his dams, bridges and palaces; some Greek and Syriac Christians and their descendants became the first communities of the Persian Church, among them the bishops of Gundeshapur and Bishapur.
nodes.src: Res Gestae Divi Saporis; Zosimus 1.36; Morony 1984; Brock 1982.

nodes.label: Soldiers and dihqans
nodes.full: The Sasanian army was drawn from the dihqans, small landowners who furnished a mounted warrior with a retinue and lived in fortified villages, and from the Daylamite infantry and the Arab and Turkish auxiliaries; their numbers and the revenues which supported them were decided by Khusrau I's reform, and a part of them, as the Persian colonists in Yemen (the Abna), remained in the lands they had conquered.
nodes.src: Tabari; Procopius, Wars 1.18; Pourshariati 2008; Daryaee 2009.

nodes.label: Jews and Christians of the border
nodes.full: The towns of the frontier, such as Nisibis, Edessa, Dara and Amida, had Syriac-speaking Christian and Jewish populations that were of mixed loyalty and, in the war, were suspected by both empires; Jewish communities in the Galilee under Heraclius saw the Persian conquest of 614 as a possible release and afterwards suffered when Heraclius returned.
nodes.src: Sebeos; Strategios; Doctrina Jacobi (c. 634); Kaegi 2003; Howard-Johnston 2010.

nodes.label: The fall of the Arsacids
nodes.full: The defeat of the last Parthian king at Hormizdagan in 224 and Ardashir’s coronation in 226 set up the Sasanian monarchy that opposed Rome for four centuries.
nodes.src: background — see the Roman–Parthian World folio (roman-parthian-world-63bc-224ad)

nodes.label: The Arab conquests
nodes.full: The Arab armies that entered Iraq and Syria in 633–636, after the exhausting war of 602–628, brought down the Sasanian empire by 651 and took most of the eastern Roman provinces.
